name: Colin Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a usual factory shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and run the plastic-tub thermoforming machine in a food-packaging plant. I left after secondary school and still need the lead to check my first tray after I change a mould. I set the heat, watch the plastic sheet pull into shape and stack the finished tubs; a thin corner means stopping the run. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. The wage is ordinary for this job, we have about two months of expenses saved and some similar plants nearby. I never use AI tools, and I prefer the printed setup sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a tidier order list is fine, but someone still has to look for a thin corner on a food tub. The forming machine is not improved by a clever sentence alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our normal wage pays the mortgage, and two months saved would cover a short gap. Some similar plants are nearby. I do not expect this mild AI change to affect my paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep forming tubs and checking the first tray with the lead. I would keep the current mortgage payment and not call the two months already saved a new contribution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the factory continuing. I can get better at the familiar mould setting without taking up an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a thin corner mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plastic stretches too far at one corner and may split when filled. I stop the belt and ask the lead to check the heat and mould before another stack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold the two months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the family a short buffer if the plant closes for any reason. I am not adding new money in this plan; I am keeping what is there.

say: A **neat** order list still leaves a food tub to inspect.
I would **keep** using the printed setup sheet and first-tray check.
think: The **usual** wage, two months saved and some local plants make work feel secure.
The **mortgage** stays in our ordinary budget.
do: **Keep** forming tubs and checking first tray with lead.
**Keep** ordinary mortgage payment and existing reserve in place.
feel: **Calm** while paid shifts and household budget continue.
S0.quote: The forming machine is not improved by a clever sentence alone.
fieldNote: **Colin** has never used AI and trusts printed settings and physical tray checks.
**Typical** pay, two months saved and some local plants support calm without inventing new saving.

steps.text: Keep forming plastic tubs and inspecting first tray with lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can plan plastic orders and schedules faster, while the forming line still needs a safe mould change. I would ask for the old and new paid setup times in writing before anyone calls the new rota efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If planning removes paid setup minutes, my wage could shrink. Two months saved let us adjust briefly, but repeated smaller weeks would reach our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the forming shift and compare four rotas with my paper setup records. If the reduction persists, I would apply only to posted nearby tub or packing jobs whose pay covers mortgage, food and travel; we would delay buying a replacement sofa until hours settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic reduction in pay. I can compare the rotas and look locally, but I would rather not gamble the family reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your paper record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write down when the old mould comes out, when the first acceptable tub appears and how many minutes the plant pays. A fast schedule cannot make a thin plastic corner safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn an AI rota tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used an AI tool; I would ask the supervisor for a printed rota and an explanation of missing hours.

**Repeated** smaller weeks would affect our mortgage despite two months saved.
do: **Compare** four paid rotas with paper mould-change records.
**Apply** after repeated cuts to posted nearby role covering household bills.
**Delay** replacement sofa if paid hours fall.

fieldNote: His **concern** is an own-wage risk from faster planning, not immediate robot replacement.
The **job** application requires repeated cuts, a posted nearby opening and adequate pay; the sofa delay is conditional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner thinking AI reaches orders in 2028 when I am forty-five, and capable hands-on robots reach tub forming around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot that changes moulds and clears tubs could leave fewer junior operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose most of my paid forming hours if the plant installs one. Two months saved would run down quickly with a mortgage and two children, and I wake at night counting those payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning while the line is paid and safe. If the plant announces cuts, I would stop the sofa purchase and ask the lender about a temporary payment plan before arrears; I would apply to a posted nearby packing or forming job only if its wage covers our bills. I would not pay for a speculative screen course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected large wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry. I have practical calls to make, but no guaranteed new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the actual new rota and ask whether a short payment pause is possible before we miss a mortgage instalment. I would not assume it will be approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work could you take nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check real posted packing or forming shifts, not a general promise of factory work. Travel and pay must still leave enough for mortgage, food and school costs.

say: 2028 **thinking** AI changes orders before tub robots around 2031.
I would **keep** paid work and seek a real nearby fallback.
think: I **expect** most junior hours to go after robot mould changes.
**Two** months saved cannot cover a long mortgage gap.
do: **Ask** lender about payment pause after announced cuts, before arrears.
**Apply** to posted nearby forming or packing job covering bills.
**Delay** sofa replacement if robot cuts are announced.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major pay loss and lost sleep.
S2.quote: Two months saved would run down quickly with a mortgage and two children, and I wake at night counting those payments.
fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected major hours loss and explicit sleeplessness about mortgage payments.
The **lender** request is not guaranteed; any job application requires a posted adequate local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches orders in 2031 when I am forty-eight, with capable hands-on robots reaching tub forming around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years lets me improve my machine setting while the wages still come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine forming hours could still shrink, but I could compare local jobs and build a little more reserve first. I would not leave paid work for a course that has no real job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the forming shifts and add new money from each paid month to an emergency account after the mortgage. If the employer offers a fully funded practical setter certificate on paid time with a stopped-machine place, and a posted nearby setter role pays our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about later hours, though the extra years give me control. I would learn a physical setting beside a trainer, not trust a screen lesson alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical training involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainer would isolate the forming machine, let me adjust a mould and test the first tub before restart. I need the full practical certificate, not a quick demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the ordinary shift and turn the course down. Our mortgage does not pause for a classroom day.

say: I would **accept** practical paid setter training if it leads to real work.
think: A **certificate** without a posted adequate local job would be too risky.
do: **Save** new money from paid forming months after mortgage.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time stopped-machine setter certificate for posted nearby role.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby setter job covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about later cuts, with years to prepare.
S3.quote: Our mortgage does not pause for a classroom day.
fieldNote: He is **resistant** to AI but accepts supervised physical setter training under paid safe conditions.
**New** savings come from wages; qualification and application depend on a posted adequate nearby setter vacancy.

steps.text: Save new pay each month after mortgage and essentials
Enrol in funded paid-time safe setter certificate for posted nearby adequate role
Apply after qualification to posted nearby setter job covering bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches orders in 2036 when I am fifty-three, with capable tub-forming robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years is time to work and prepare, not a reason to pretend I can retire at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, but we will still need an income. I might be better at the mould by then; I cannot assume that alone guarantees a job after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid forming shifts and put a new amount from each full wage into savings after bills. I would ask the lead for more supervised mould-setting practice; if the plant offers a fully funded practical setter certificate on paid time and a posted nearby role at bill-covering pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a distant loss while current paid work looks steady. I will take the wage we know and check each promised training place before changing direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI controls by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools and would first ask for an in-person demonstration on a stopped machine. Watching one would not mean I had learned to use the control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no setter vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the forming job while it pays safely, then check posted nearby packing work if hours are cut. I would compare the actual wage with mortgage and travel costs.

think: **Wages** remain necessary after age fifty-six even if the children are older.
**Mould** skill alone will not guarantee a future role.
do: **Save** new money from full forming wages after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time safe setter certificate for posted nearby adequate role.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby setter job covering bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant change with current wages intact.
S4.quote: Ten years is time to work and prepare, not a reason to pretend I can retire at fifty-six.

His **course** and job application remain conditional on funded paid safe practice and posted local adequate pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable tub-forming robots around 2031 could remove most of my paid hours before the mortgage is smaller. A lender payment plan and real nearby work at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a family does between the last paid forming shift and the first new job. I would check a real posted wage before I moved plants. The first plastic tub has to hold food, and my next wage has to hold our household.

headlineQuote: The first plastic tub has to hold food, and my next wage has to hold our household.
portrait: **Colin**, forty-three, is a junior plastic-tub forming operator with secondary schooling and two school-age children.
His **typical** wage, two-month reserve and some nearby plants support stability while a mortgage still matters.
He **never** uses AI and trusts printed settings, physical first-tub checks and supervised practical instruction.
**Fast** robots threaten his paid hours; longer notice permits new saving and a conditional paid setter qualification.
biggestWorry: **Fast** forming robots around 2031 could remove most junior paid hours before the family has enough mortgage breathing room.
whatWouldHelp: A **possible** temporary mortgage payment plan and posted nearby bill-covering work would help after lost shifts.
